title: Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) Agar

references.label: Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media

purpose: A selective and differential medium used to isolate and differentiate enteric pathogens, particularly Shigella and Salmonella species, from a mixed fecal or environmental sample based on sugar fermentation, lysine decarboxylation, and hydrogen sulfide production.

reference.label: Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media
Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media

preparationSummary: Suspend the dehydrated powder in distilled/deionized water and heat with agitation just until dissolved; XLD agar should not be autoclaved (prolonged heat degrades the selective and differential components), so it is typically boiled briefly and poured directly.

sterilization.value: not autoclaved — typically brought just to boiling to dissolve, per manufacturer instructions, since autoclaving degrades the medium's selective/differential performance

reference.label: Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media

storage: Store prepared plates refrigerated (commonly 2-8°C) in sealed bags, protected from light; XLD plates are generally used relatively soon after pouring.

shelfLife.value: manufacturer-stated shelf life varies by product and storage condition, and is typically shorter than simpler general-purpose media

expectedAppearance: Translucent red/pink medium; colonies vary by organism (see reactions).
qualityControl: Confirm sterility (no growth on an uninoculated control plate) and verify expected colony morphology/color with known reference organisms before use in diagnostic work.

reactions.reaction: Typically red/pink colonies with black centers (H2S production)
Typically red colonies without black centers (non-lysine-decarboxylating, non-H2S)

reactions.organismOrGroup: Lactose/sucrose-fermenting coliforms (e.g. many E. coli strains)
reactions.reaction: Typically yellow colonies (acid production from sugar fermentation)

manufacturerNotes: Interpretation depends on the interplay of sugar fermentation, lysine decarboxylation, and H2S production together — no single color change should be interpreted in isolation.
